title: Restraint of speech (Rule 6)
hook: even good words should be few
tomorrow: in a house that runs on a strict schedule, who goes first?

segments.voice: Tools of good works: Benedict's toolbox, with never despair of God's mercy saved for last. One small tool on that list was don't love much talking. He gives it a whole chapter.
screen: `NEVER DESPAIR OF GOD'S MERCY.` → `ONE SMALL TOOL, A WHOLE CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: At the end of a song, a good choir cuts off together, and for a second the room keeps ringing. Nobody claps yet. That second belongs to the music. Group chats almost never have one. Benedict wants more of that second in a day. His chapter on speech opens with a psalm, in the King James: "I will keep my mouth with a bridle." Then he says something that stops a reader short. He isn't only ruling out gossip and cruelty. Even good talk, holy talk, the kind that builds people up, should be rare. So why ration the good words?
screen: `THE ROOM KEEPS RINGING.` → `A BRIDLE FOR THE MOUTH.` → `EVEN GOOD WORDS, FEW?`

segments.voice: His reasoning goes like this. If we should sometimes hold back even from good words for the sake of silence, how much more from bad ones. He leans on Proverbs: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin." More talk, more room to go wrong. Even a monk who is good at holy conversation, he says, should rarely be given the floor. Then a picture of the community. Speaking and teaching belong to the teacher; being quiet and listening belong to the learner. So when a monk needs something from the abbot, he asks humbly, in few words. Crude jokes and idle chatter Benedict shuts out everywhere. Notice what this chapter is not. It isn't a vow of total silence: the same Rule has monks singing psalms together and reading aloud at meals. And it isn't contempt for words. It's a sense that words are heavy, and that a person who talks less hears more: the brother across the table, the reading, God. The chapter's Latin title points to taciturnity, the habit of keeping quiet. Not muteness. Restraint. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in Benedict's school, silence is a way of listening, not a punishment. It's the difference between filling every pause and letting a pause do some of the work, like that ringing second after the choir stops.
screen: `EVEN GOOD WORDS, SOMETIMES HELD BACK.` · `THE TEACHER SPEAKS; THE LEARNER LISTENS.` · `NOT A VOW OF TOTAL SILENCE.` · `SILENCE AS A WAY OF LISTENING.` · then, large: `FEWER WORDS.`

segments.voice: Say one true sentence out loud, short and plain, something you mean. Then stop, and listen to the room ring after it: the hum, the traffic, your breath. Stay inside that ringing second for the whole sit, and let any new sentence go unfinished.
Restraint of speech. Benedict's chapter on keeping words few, even good ones, so there's room to listen.
Carry this: fewer words, so the true one can stand on its own. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries, silence is kept at set times and places, and monks and nuns speak sparingly, while still singing the psalms and reading aloud together.
